content:
Global stock markets are heading for their worst run in more than three years as a sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence shares spread from Wall Street across Asia on Friday, wiping out trillions of dollars in value and sending investors scrambling for the safety of government bonds and the dollar.

The MSCI All Country World Index, a broad barometer of global equities, fell 0.6 percent and was on course for a seventh consecutive day of declines, its longest losing streak since September 2023, according to [Bloomberg's markets coverage](https://www.swissinfo.ch/eng/stocks-set-for-worst-run-since-2023,-havens-gain:-markets-wrap/92410554). Asia took the heaviest blow. The MSCI Asia Pacific benchmark slid 3.2 percent and was set for its worst week since March 2020, while emerging-market stocks extended their fall from a June peak to 20 percent, putting them on the edge of a technical bear market.

In the United States, the rout deepened on Thursday. The S&P 500 dropped 2 percent for a sixth straight loss, its longest slide in two and a half years, and the index at the heart of millions of American retirement accounts is now down 8.2 percent from its all-time high set last month, according to the Associated Press. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,101 points, or 2.2 percent, to 49,097, closing below 50,000 for the first time since June and taking its four-day decline to 3,250 points. The Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 percent, and more than 90 percent of the stocks in the S&P 500 ended the day lower.

Asia opened on Friday to a sea of red. Japan's Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.54 percent and the broader Topix lost 2.75 percent. South Korea's Kospi fell more than 4 percent, dropping back below the 5,000 mark. Taiwan's Taiex plunged nearly 6 percent, putting it on course for its worst week since 1991. The selling hit the region's chip giants hardest, with SK Hynix and Samsung leading the declines in Seoul.

The paradox at the centre of the week is Anthropic. The maker of the Claude chatbot completed the largest initial public offering in history on Thursday, selling shares at 83 dollars apiece and closing 17 percent higher at 97.17 dollars, for a market value of roughly 1.76 trillion dollars. Many traders had hoped the blockbuster debut would steady nerves. Instead, Anthropic's own shares slipped in after-hours trading, and the rest of the market kept falling.

"The market is clearly unhappy, and AI sits firmly at the center of the selling," Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone Group, told Bloomberg. Investors are asking a question that would have sounded absurd a year ago: whether the vast sums being spent and borrowed to build artificial intelligence can ever earn enough to justify themselves. Nvidia, the company at the heart of the boom, erased an early gain of 4.7 percent on Thursday and closed down 3.3 percent, despite reporting earnings that beat expectations. The chipmaker has now shed hundreds of billions of dollars in market value in less than two weeks.

The doubts go beyond valuations. California has opened an investigation into whether China improperly obtained Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information, and documents from the US House of Representatives showed that a Commerce Department sub-agency approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese firms between December 2025 and May 2026. The chip-export question has become a political fault line in Washington, as [Global Wire reported earlier this week](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-congress-report-china-nvidia-chips-ai-weapons-november-2026). AMD plunged 7.72 percent on Thursday after a short-seller report alleged its firmware continued to reach a Chinese server maker on the US entity list, a claim the company denied.

Interest rates are adding to the pressure. Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting leaned hawkish, with most officials seeing inflation as the bigger risk, and the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note stood at 5.02 percent as investors moved into bonds. The VIX, Wall Street's fear gauge, jumped nearly 16 percent in a single day to 28.44.

"Investors are questioning whether frontier AI is becoming a hugely successful technology but an increasingly difficult business in which to earn attractive returns," Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets, told Bloomberg. Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist at Societe Generale, said the sell-off reflected worries that AI-led growth is slowing and that the "peak growth phase" may have passed.

For ordinary savers, the damage is real but not yet catastrophic. The S&P 500 remains far above its levels of a year ago, and the index has fallen 8.2 percent from its peak, a correction, not a crash. But the speed of the decline, and the fact that it is led by the very stocks that drove the market to record highs, is what has rattled traders. As [Warren Buffett's record Berkshire donation showed this week](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/warren-buffett-5-47-billion-berkshire-donation-november-2026), even the most seasoned investors are repositioning for a different kind of market.

What happens next depends on three things traders will watch in the coming days. First, whether the Federal Reserve signals any relief on interest rates at its December meeting. Second, whether the AI industry can show that its enormous spending on data centres is turning into real profits rather than just bigger bills. And third, whether the political fight over advanced chips reaching China escalates further, adding a new layer of risk to the world's most valuable companies. Until one of those questions gets a reassuring answer, the selling may not be over.
summary: Global stocks are heading for their worst run since 2023 as an AI-led sell-off spread from Wall Street to Asia, with the S&P 500 down for a sixth straight session and the Nikkei tumbling 4.5 percent, even as Anthropic completed the largest IPO in history.
title: Global stocks head for worst run since 2023 as AI sell-off spreads from Wall Street to Asia
